    "text": "1.1 PROBABILITY MODELS\n\nProbability theory is concerned with the analysis of random phenomena. The outcome of a random experiment cannot be determined with certainty, but the set of all possible outcomes can be described. For example, if we flip a coin, the outcome could be Heads or Tails. If we roll a die, the outcome could be any integer from 1 to 6. A probability model is a mathematical description of such an experiment. It provides a formal framework for understanding and predicting the behavior of random events. The most common framework for probability is based on measure theory, which provides a rigorous foundation for defining probabilities on a wide variety of sets, including continuous spaces like $\\mathbb{R}^n$. However, for introductory purposes, a more intuitive understanding of probability can often suffice. We will, however, introduce the formal definitions early in the book.\n\nThe basic building blocks of a probability model are the sample space, the set of all possible outcomes, and the events, subsets of the sample space whose probability we want to quantify. For example, for a coin toss, the sample space is $\\Omega = \\{H, T\\}$, and an event could be \"the coin lands Heads.\" In a more complex scenario, such as selecting a real number from the interval $[0, 1]$, the sample space is $\\Omega = [0, 1]$, and an event might be \"the selected number is in $(a, b)$,\" where $0 \\le a < b \\le 1$. The collection of all such events for which we can assign a probability is denoted by $\\mathcal{F}$.",

    "text": "Definition 1.1. A probability model is a triple $(\\Omega, \\mathcal{F}, P)$ where\n1.  $\\Omega$ is the sample space, the set of all possible outcomes.\n2.  $\\mathcal{F}$ is a $\\sigma$-field of events on $\\Omega$, which means:\n    (a) $\\emptyset \\in \\mathcal{F}$ and $\\Omega \\in \\mathcal{F}$.\n    (b) If $A \\in \\mathcal{F}$, then $A^c \\in \\mathcal{F}$. (Closure under complementation)\n    (c) If $(A_i)_{i=1}^\\infty$ is a sequence of events in $\\mathcal{F}$, then $\\bigcup_{i=1}^\\infty A_i \\in \\mathcal{F}$. (Closure under countable unions)\n3.  $P: \\mathcal{F} \\to \\mathbb{R}$ is a probability measure (or probability distribution) satisfying the following axioms:\n    (P1) $P(\\Omega) = 1$.\n    (P2) $P(A) \\ge 0$ for all $A \\in \\mathcal{F}$.\n    (P3) If $(A_i)_{i=1}^\\infty$ is a sequence of disjoint events in $\\mathcal{F}$ (i.e., $A_i \\cap A_j = \\emptyset$ for $i \\ne j$), then\n    $$P\\left(\\bigcup_{i=1}^\\infty A_i\\right) = \\sum_{i=1}^\\infty P(A_i).$$",

    "text": "The set $\\Omega$ is called the sample space. Its elements $\\omega \\in \\Omega$ are called outcomes, sample points, or realizations. An event is a subset of $\\Omega$ to which a probability is assigned. For mathematical convenience, not all subsets of $\\Omega$ are necessarily events. For example, in the continuous setting, it is generally not possible to assign probabilities to all subsets of $\\mathbb{R}$. The collection of events $\\mathcal{F}$ is thus a subcollection of all subsets of $\\Omega$ that satisfies certain properties. These properties, listed in Definition 1.1.2(a)-(c), ensure that $\\mathcal{F}$ is closed under the standard set operations that arise in probability theory (complements, unions, intersections). A collection of events $\\mathcal{F}$ that satisfies (1) and (2) is called a $\\sigma$-field.",
